items.prompt: What makes a regulator a different kind of stakeholder than a user or the business, per this unit?
choices: Regulators are just another name for users with more permissions
A regulator mostly shows up after the fact, asking the system to prove something about its own past behavior — not to use it right now
Regulators only care about system uptime
There is no meaningful difference — all stakeholders want the same thing
items.explanation: Users and the business judge a system by what it does now (fast, cheap, correct). A regulator typically shows up later — during an audit, an incident, or a subject request — and asks the system to prove what it did in the past, which is a different engineering demand entirely.
items.reference:
Userdo the thing now, fast
Businessdo it cheaply, ship fast
Regulatorprove, later, it was done lawfully

Why: proving something later is a fundamentally different problem than doing it correctly right now.

items.prompt: A fintech's platform is fast and reliable for users, but can't prove what happened to a specific customer's data six months ago when an auditor asks. What does this unit say about that gap?
choices: The system is fine — being reliable for users is all that matters
The system can be functionally flawless for its actual users and still fail an audit, because it was never built to remember its own past
This only happens to poorly engineered systems, never well-built ones
Auditors never actually ask about specific customers
items.explanation: A system judged only against 'does it work right now' can be excellent by that measure and still fail completely against 'can it prove what it did' — because nothing about correctness-right-now guarantees the system kept a record of the past.
items.reference:
Userdo the thing now, fast
Businessdo it cheaply, ship fast
Regulatorprove, later, it was done lawfully

Why: proving something later is a fundamentally different problem than doing it correctly right now.

items.prompt: Which four properties does this unit say regulated-data architectures converge on, regardless of which specific regulation (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, SOX) applies?
choices: Speed, cost, uptime, and scalability
Auditability, minimality, boundedness, and immutability of evidence
Encryption, redundancy, load balancing, and caching
Popularity, documentation quality, test coverage, and code style
items.explanation: Different regimes have different specific rules, but their architectural asks converge on: proving who did what and when (auditability), exposing only what's needed to who needs it (minimality), giving data a lawful lifetime (boundedness), and keeping the record of the past from being quietly rewritten (immutability of evidence).
items.reference:
🔎 Auditability — who did what, when
🎯 Minimality — least data, fewest people
⏳ Boundedness — a lawful lifetime, then gone
🔒 Immutability — the past can't be rewritten

Why: these four are structural properties of how data flows and is stored, not a feature toggle.

items.prompt: What does 'immutability of evidence' specifically protect against, as distinct from auditability alone?
choices: It protects against the system being too slow to log events
It protects against the audit trail itself being quietly edited after the fact — without it, a record that exists can still be rewritten into a false story
It means data can never be deleted for any reason
It only applies to publicly visible data, not internal records
items.explanation: Auditability says a trail exists; immutability of evidence says that trail can't be silently rewritten later. A mutable log that records everything is still worthless as evidence if anyone can edit it after the fact.
items.reference:
🔎 Auditability — who did what, when
🎯 Minimality — least data, fewest people
⏳ Boundedness — a lawful lifetime, then gone
🔒 Immutability — the past can't be rewritten

Why: these four are structural properties of how data flows and is stored, not a feature toggle.

items.prompt: A system logs every access to PII and never edits those logs, but keeps every record forever with no deletion process. Which of the four properties is missing?
choices: Auditability
Boundedness — regulated data needs a defined lawful lifetime, not indefinite retention just because deleting things is scary
Immutability of evidence
Nothing is missing; keeping everything forever is always safest
items.explanation: Auditability and immutability are satisfied here, but boundedness is a separate property: data needs a defined, enforced lifetime. Keeping everything forever isn't automatically compliant — many regimes require deletion or anonymization on a schedule.
items.reference:
🔎 Auditability — who did what, when
🎯 Minimality — least data, fewest people
⏳ Boundedness — a lawful lifetime, then gone
🔒 Immutability — the past can't be rewritten

Why: these four are structural properties of how data flows and is stored, not a feature toggle.

items.prompt: Per L1's chart of where regulated data flows, which surfaces tend to have the MOST services touching PII — the raw database, or logs/exports/support tooling?
choices: The raw database always has the most exposure
Logs, analytics exports, and support tooling — surfaces nobody thought to scope as carefully as the primary datastore
All surfaces have identical exposure by design
Only third-party APIs ever touch PII
items.explanation: The uncomfortable finding most teams get on their first real inventory: fewer services touch storage directly, while more touch app logs, analytics exports, and support tools — surfaces that don't get the same scrutiny as the primary database.
items.reference:
🗄️ Storage: fewest services touch it directly
📜 Logs, exports, support tools: most services touch these

Why: minimality has to be designed for the whole exposure surface, not assumed from securing the database alone.

items.prompt: Why does this unit call the exposure-surface finding (more PII in logs/exports than in the database itself) 'uncomfortable' rather than surprising in a good way?
choices: Because it means the database is poorly designed
Because teams that secure the primary database well can still leak PII broadly through channels — logs, exports, support tools — that never got the same scrutiny
Because it means logging should be disabled entirely
Because it proves regulators only care about databases
items.explanation: It's uncomfortable because a team can feel secure — 'we locked down the database' — while PII quietly spreads through channels that were never inventoried or gated the same way, which is exactly what an audit tends to surface first.
items.reference:
🗄️ Storage: fewest services touch it directly
📜 Logs, exports, support tools: most services touch these

Why: minimality has to be designed for the whole exposure surface, not assumed from securing the database alone.

items.prompt: Why does this unit argue that 'we'll add compliance later' doesn't really work, rather than just being inconvenient?
choices: Because compliance software is always too expensive to add at all
Because these properties are structural — retrofitting an audit trail onto a system that overwrites rows in place means history before the retrofit is already permanently gone
Because regulators forbid teams from ever changing their architecture
It works fine; timing makes no real difference
items.explanation: Auditability, minimality, boundedness, and immutability are properties of how data flows and is stored from the start. A retrofit can't recover history that a mutable, overwrite-in-place system already destroyed before the retrofit shipped.
items.reference:
Add later→History before the retrofit is already gone

Why: these are architecture decisions made early, not paperwork added at the end.

items.prompt: A team plans to retrofit field-level access control onto a system where five services already read the raw PII table directly. What does this unit say about the actual cost of that retrofit?
choices: It's trivial — just add one new check and every service benefits equally
It means untangling five separate services' worth of existing assumptions about that data, not just writing one new check
It's impossible and the system must be rebuilt from scratch
Only the newest of the five services needs any changes
items.explanation: Each of the five services was built assuming direct access to the raw table. Gating that access after the fact means finding and updating every one of those assumptions, which is a much larger and riskier job than writing the gate itself.
items.reference:
Add later→History before the retrofit is already gone

Why: these are architecture decisions made early, not paperwork added at the end.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, why couldn't the fintech team answer the auditor's request about who touched customer SSNs over the past year?
choices: They refused to cooperate with the auditor
Rows were overwritten in place with no history kept, and access logs rotated out after 30 days — nothing was built to remember
The SSNs had never actually been stored anywhere
The auditor's request was technically impossible to satisfy under any architecture
items.explanation: Mutable rows with no history, and logs that rotate out after a month, mean the system simply has no memory of what happened more than 30 days ago — not because it's impossible to build, but because this particular system wasn't designed to keep it.
items.reference:
🗄️ Mutable rows, no history kept
📜 Logs rotate out after 30 days
🤷 No record of who read which field, ever

Why: a system can be excellent for its users and still have no memory of its own past.

items.prompt: The team in L1's scenario was 'proud of their architecture' — fast, scalable, frequent deploys. What does this unit say that pride actually measured?
choices: It measured everything a regulator would also care about
It measured how well the system served users and the business — a different, narrower measure than whether the system could prove its own past behavior
Nothing; the pride was entirely unjustified even for users
It measured compliance readiness specifically
items.explanation: Speed, scale, and deploy frequency are real strengths — for the audience the team was actually building for. None of those properties say anything about whether the system can prove what happened to a specific record six months ago, which is the regulator's distinct question.
items.reference:
🗄️ Mutable rows, no history kept
📜 Logs rotate out after 30 days
🤷 No record of who read which field, ever

Why: a system can be excellent for its users and still have no memory of its own past.

items.prompt: Per L1, what's the practical difference between how a `PUBLIC` field and a `PII_RESTRICTED` field like an SSN should typically be handled?
choices: No difference — all fields should be treated identically for simplicity
A `PUBLIC` field can be read broadly, while a `PII_RESTRICTED` field should be limited to named services only, with every access logged
PUBLIC fields need MORE logging than PII_RESTRICTED fields
Classification only matters for fields stored in a separate database
items.explanation: Classification is what makes minimality enforceable in practice: broadly-readable fields need no special gate, while restricted fields like SSNs get narrowed access and logged access, so 'need to know' means something concrete instead of a vague policy.
items.reference:
PUBLICany authenticated service
INTERNALdocumented business need
PII_RESTRICTEDnamed services, every access logged

Why: classification is what turns 'need to know' from a policy phrase into an enforceable default.

items.prompt: Why does even a service that's DENIED access to a PII_RESTRICTED field still generate a logged event, per this unit's framing?
choices: It doesn't — denied reads are never logged
Because whether a field was ever even attempted to be read is itself something a regulator or investigator can ask about, regardless of the outcome
Logging denied reads is purely for debugging performance issues
Only successful writes are ever logged, never reads
items.explanation: An access attempt — allowed or denied — is itself a fact worth recording. Logging only successful reads would hide exactly the kind of repeated-attempt pattern that matters most for investigating misuse.
items.reference:
PUBLICany authenticated service
INTERNALdocumented business need
PII_RESTRICTEDnamed services, every access logged

Why: classification is what turns 'need to know' from a policy phrase into an enforceable default.

items.prompt: Why doesn't a `last_modified_by` column on a table satisfy auditability, even though it does record who last changed the row?
choices: It does satisfy auditability completely on its own
It only ever holds the most recent change — everything before the latest write is already forgotten, which fails an auditor asking about the last 12 months
Column names starting with `last_` are forbidden by most regulations
It only works for numeric fields, not text
items.explanation: A single mutable field is overwritten on every change, so it can only ever answer 'who changed this last,' never 'who touched this over the past year.' Auditability requires the whole history, not just the latest fact.
items.reference:
🗄️ last_modified_by: only the most recent fact
📜 Append-only log: the whole history, nothing overwritten

Why: an append-only event log keeps the whole history; current state is built by folding it forward.

items.prompt: In the append-only audit log pattern, how does the operational database (current-state table) relate to the log?
choices: The log replaces the operational database entirely
The log sits alongside the operational database as the system's memory of its own past — the DB still holds current state, unchanged
The operational database is deleted once the log exists
They must always be the exact same physical table
items.explanation: The append-only log doesn't replace how the system serves current reads/writes — it adds a durable record of what happened over time, alongside the existing operational data store.
items.reference:
🗄️ last_modified_by: only the most recent fact
📜 Append-only log: the whole history, nothing overwritten

Why: an append-only event log keeps the whole history; current state is built by folding it forward.

items.prompt: Per L2, how does a correction to a mistaken audit-log entry get made, if the log is truly append-only?
choices: The original event is edited in place to fix the mistake
As a brand-new appended event describing the correction — the original event is never edited
Corrections aren't allowed; mistaken entries stay wrong forever with no way to note it
Only a database administrator may edit past entries, but no one else
items.explanation: Append-only means exactly that — corrections are new events layered on top of the history, not edits to what already happened. This is what keeps the log trustworthy as a record of the actual past, including its own mistakes and their corrections.
items.reference:
🗄️ last_modified_by: only the most recent fact
📜 Append-only log: the whole history, nothing overwritten

Why: an append-only event log keeps the whole history; current state is built by folding it forward.

items.prompt: A team lets support staff edit a 'reason' text field on already-written audit events, so unclear original entries can be clarified later. Per L2's checkpoint, is this a safe convenience?
choices: Yes, editing metadata fields is always fine as long as the core action/actor/timestamp stay fixed
No — any editable field on an already-written event breaks the append-only guarantee, since it lets someone rewrite the story after the fact
Yes, but only if a manager approves each edit verbally
It's safe as long as the edits happen within 24 hours of the original entry
items.explanation: The moment any field on a stored event can be edited, the log can no longer be trusted as an unaltered record — an editable 'reason' field is exactly the kind of quiet backdoor that defeats the whole point of append-only.
items.reference:
❌ Editing a stored event's field: breaks append-only
✅ A correction is a NEW appended event, never an edit

Why: the fix isn't banning corrections — it's making every correction its own new, appended event.

items.prompt: What's the correct way to fix an unclear 'reason' on an already-written audit event, per L2, without breaking append-only?
choices: Append a new event stating the original event's reason was updated, by whom, and when — leaving the original event unchanged
Delete the original event and write a replacement with the corrected reason
Directly overwrite the reason field, since it's just metadata not the core action
Corrections are impossible under append-only, so the field should never exist
items.explanation: A correction is a new event layered on top — it references the original by id and states what changed, who changed it, and when, while the original event stays exactly as it was originally recorded.
items.reference:
❌ Editing a stored event's field: breaks append-only
✅ A correction is a NEW appended event, never an edit

Why: the fix isn't banning corrections — it's making every correction its own new, appended event.

items.prompt: A new analytics service asks for read access to the customer table 'to build some dashboards,' without naming specific fields. Per L2, what should the access gate default to?
choices: Grant full access immediately, and revoke fields later if someone objects
The lowest classification that satisfies the request — PUBLIC fields only — until specific higher-classification fields are named and reviewed
Deny the service entirely until a formal legal review, even for PUBLIC fields
Grant whatever the requesting engineer's manager approves verbally
items.explanation: Minimality means the default posture is exclusion, not broad-grant-then-revoke. A vague request like 'to build dashboards' doesn't name a business need for restricted fields, so the gate should default to the least access that satisfies what was actually asked for.
items.reference:
🚪 Default: exclusion until a specific need is named
❌ Not: grant broadly, revoke later if someone notices

Why: revocation-after-the-fact reproduces the untracked exposure surface minimality exists to prevent.

items.prompt: Why does L2 specifically reject a 'grant broad access now, revoke later if someone complains' approach to a new service's data access?
choices: Because revoking access is technically impossible in most systems
Because that pattern is exactly what produces the untracked, unscoped exposure surface (logs, exports, tools) L1's chart showed
Because it's slower than granting narrow access upfront
Because regulators explicitly ban all future access changes
items.explanation: Grant-then-revoke means the system runs with unnecessarily broad access for however long it takes someone to notice and object — which is precisely how PII ends up spread across surfaces nobody scoped, as L1's chart illustrated.
items.reference:
🚪 Default: exclusion until a specific need is named
❌ Not: grant broadly, revoke later if someone notices

Why: revocation-after-the-fact reproduces the untracked exposure surface minimality exists to prevent.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does even the deletion step of a retention scheduler need to be logged?
choices: It doesn't — deletion is an exemption from auditability, not part of it
Because deleting regulated data is exactly the kind of event a regulator asks about — proving what was deleted and when is itself a compliance requirement
Only additions need to be logged, never removals
Logging deletions is only needed for financial data, never other PII
items.explanation: A regulator can ask 'prove you actually deleted what you said you would, and when.' If deletions aren't logged, there's no way to answer that question — deletion doesn't opt a system out of auditability, it's one more event the trail needs to cover.
items.reference:
📆 Retention policy attached to classification at write time
🤖 Scheduler runs regularly, checks deadlines
📝 Deletion itself is a logged event, not an exemption

Why: boundedness needs a policy attached to classification, plus a process that actually enforces the deadline.

items.prompt: What does L2 say a retention policy needs to be attached to, in order for boundedness to actually work?
choices: Nothing — a single global deletion deadline works for all data equally
The data's classification at write time, so different kinds of data can have appropriately different lawful lifetimes
The engineer who happened to write the code that created the record
The current disk usage of the database
items.explanation: Different classifications typically carry different lawful retention windows. Attaching the policy to classification at write time means the system knows each record's deadline from the moment it's created, rather than needing a manual audit to figure it out later.
items.reference:
📆 Retention policy attached to classification at write time
🤖 Scheduler runs regularly, checks deadlines
📝 Deletion itself is a logged event, not an exemption

Why: boundedness needs a policy attached to classification, plus a process that actually enforces the deadline.

items.prompt: In L2's scenario, a written data-handling policy said access should be need-to-know, but every service's database credential could already SELECT every column. What does this show?
choices: The policy was doing real, active work protecting the data
A policy document that nothing consults at request time isn't a control — it's something the team can point to after the fact, not something that actually restricts access
Database credentials are irrelevant to minimality
The problem only exists if the policy is poorly worded
items.explanation: A control has to be checked at the moment access happens. A policy that's never consulted by any code path is documentation, not enforcement — it doesn't change what any service can actually do.
items.reference:
Policy document≠Enforced gate in code

Why: minimality has to be enforced structurally, checked at request time, not asked-for-nicely in a wiki page.

items.prompt: What does L2 say has to change for minimality to move from 'hope' to an actual control?
choices: Nothing needs to change — well-written policy documents are sufficient on their own
Data needs to be classified, and access to each classification gated in code that runs on every request, not left to a policy nobody consults
Only hiring more compliance staff to manually review requests fixes it
Switching to a different database vendor automatically solves it
items.explanation: The shift is from 'a rule described in prose' to 'a rule enforced in code, checked at request time' — classification plus a gate is what makes need-to-know something the system actually does, rather than something the team merely intends.
items.reference:
Policy document≠Enforced gate in code

Why: minimality has to be enforced structurally, checked at request time, not asked-for-nicely in a wiki page.

items.prompt: How does L2 relate the append-only audit log to event sourcing, as covered in architecture/event-driven-architecture?
choices: They're unrelated ideas that happen to share the word 'event'
It's the same underlying idea (append rather than overwrite, derive current state by folding events forward), applied specifically to access/change events rather than domain state
Event sourcing replaces the need for an audit log entirely
Audit logs and event sourcing are mutually exclusive patterns
items.explanation: Both patterns share the core mechanic — append immutable facts, derive current state by replaying them — just applied to different content: event sourcing typically models business/domain state, while the audit log here specifically tracks access and change events.
items.reference:
Event sourcing→domain state
Audit log→access & change events

Why: same append-forward mechanic, applied to a different kind of fact.

items.prompt: This unit says the audit log doesn't replace the operational database. What does event sourcing's 'derive current state by folding events forward' idea correspond to, in the audit-log version of the pattern?
choices: It corresponds to deleting the operational database once the log exists
It corresponds to the log's events being derivable into a history view (who touched what, when) while the operational database still directly serves current-state reads
It has no correspondence — the two patterns don't actually share this idea
It means the audit log must be replayed on every single API request
items.explanation: The shared idea is 'append immutable facts, derive views by folding them forward' — but the audit log's derived view is a history/trail (who accessed or changed what, when), not the operational current-state itself, which the regular database continues to serve directly.
items.reference:
Event sourcing→domain state
Audit log→access & change events

Why: same append-forward mechanic, applied to a different kind of fact.

items.prompt: Implement a simplified `append(log, event)` that appends an event to an array-based log, where each stored event gets a `seq` (its index in the array) and a `prevHash` equal to the previous event's `hash`, or `"GENESIS"` if it's the first event. For this exercise, compute `hash` simply as `` `h${seq}` `` (a placeholder, not real hashing) so the test can check the chain-linking logic without needing a crypto library. Return the newly stored event.

tests.description: first event gets seq 0 and prevHash GENESIS
tests.expr: (() => { const log = []; const e = append(log, { actor: 'a' }); return expect(e.seq).toBe(0) })()

tests.description: first event prevHash is GENESIS
tests.expr: (() => { const log = []; const e = append(log, { actor: 'a' }); return expect(e.prevHash).toBe('GENESIS') })()

tests.description: second event chains to first event's hash
tests.expr: (() => { const log = []; const e1 = append(log, { actor: 'a' }); const e2 = append(log, { actor: 'b' }); return expect(e2.prevHash).toBe(e1.hash) })()

tests.description: second event gets seq 1
tests.expr: (() => { const log = []; append(log, { actor: 'a' }); const e2 = append(log, { actor: 'b' }); return expect(e2.seq).toBe(1) })()

tests.description: appended event is pushed into the log array
tests.expr: (() => { const log = []; append(log, { actor: 'a' }); return expect(log.length).toBe(1) })()

items.explanation: Each event's position (seq) and its link to the previous event (prevHash) are what turn a flat array into a chain — every event after the first points back to the one before it, so the log's order can't be silently reshuffled without breaking that link.
items.reference:
0 prevHash: GENESIS
1 prevHash: hash of event 0
2 prevHash: hash of event 1

Why: each event's hash depends on the one before it, forming an unbroken chain back to genesis.

items.prompt: Implement `verifyChain(log)` that walks an array of stored events (each with `seq`, `prevHash`, `hash`) and returns `true` only if every event's `prevHash` correctly equals the hash of the event immediately before it (and the first event's `prevHash` is `"GENESIS"`). Return `false` on the first mismatch found.

tests.description: an untampered 3-event chain verifies true
a broken link in the middle returns false
a wrong first prevHash returns false
an empty log is trivially valid

items.explanation: Walking forward and tracking 'what the prevHash should be' catches any broken link immediately — a single tampered or reordered event changes what the next event's prevHash should have pointed to, which this loop flags on the very next iteration.
items.reference:
0 prevHash: GENESIS
1 prevHash: hash of event 0
2 prevHash: hash of event 1

Why: each event's hash depends on the one before it, forming an unbroken chain back to genesis.

items.prompt: Implement `gateField(value, classification, grantedClassifications)`: return `value` unchanged if `classification` is present in the `grantedClassifications` array, otherwise return the string `"[REDACTED]"`.

tests.description: granted classification returns the real value
ungranted classification returns REDACTED
empty grant list redacts everything
PUBLIC field with PUBLIC granted passes through

items.explanation: The gate's whole job is a single membership check: does this caller's granted set include this field's classification. Everything else (logging, per-field iteration) is orchestration around this one decision.
items.reference:
caller scope includes classification?
✅ yes→real value
❌ no→[REDACTED], access still logged

Why: the gate decides visibility per field, independent of whether the read gets logged.

items.prompt: Implement `gateRecord(record, fields, grantedClassifications)` where `fields` is an array of `{ name, classification }`. Return a new object with every field name mapped to its value (if the classification is granted) or `"[REDACTED]"` (if not). Do not mutate the original `record`.

tests.description: mixed access: some fields pass, some redacted
restricted field redacted when not granted
original record is not mutated
all fields granted returns full record

items.explanation: Building a fresh object field by field, rather than editing the input, avoids accidentally leaking the original reference (and its unredacted values) to a caller who only asked for the gated view.
items.reference:
caller scope includes classification?
✅ yes→real value
❌ no→[REDACTED], access still logged

Why: the gate decides visibility per field, independent of whether the read gets logged.

items.prompt: Implement `isPastDeadline(createdAtIso, retentionMonths, asOfIso)`: return `true` if at least `retentionMonths` full calendar months have passed between `createdAtIso` and `asOfIso`, else `false`. Compute months as `(asOfYear - createdYear) * 12 + (asOfMonth - createdMonth)` (0-indexed months, matching JS Date.getMonth()).

tests.description: exactly at the deadline counts as past due
one month before deadline is not past due
well past deadline is past due
freshly created record is not past due

items.explanation: Computing elapsed months as a year-difference times 12 plus a month-difference avoids the trap of trying to divide raw millisecond differences by an 'average month length,' which drifts and can misclassify records near their exact deadline.
items.reference:
📆 elapsed = (asOfYear - createdYear) × 12 + (asOfMonth - createdMonth)
⏳ past deadline when elapsed >= retentionMonths

Why: a retention deadline is a calendar concept, not a raw duration — computing it in months avoids drift.

items.prompt: Implement `classifyForEnforcement(record)` where `record` has `pastDeadline` (boolean) and `legalHold` (boolean). Return `"delete"` if past deadline and no legal hold, `"held"` if past deadline and under legal hold, or `"leave"` if not past deadline (regardless of legal hold).

tests.description: past deadline, no hold: delete
past deadline, held: held
not past deadline, no hold: leave
not past deadline, held: leave (deadline hasn't arrived yet)

items.explanation: The deadline check comes first: a record that isn't past its deadline yet is left alone regardless of legal hold, because the hold only matters as an override to a deletion that would otherwise happen. Once past deadline, the hold decides between 'delete' and 'held.'
items.reference:
📆 elapsed = (asOfYear - createdYear) × 12 + (asOfMonth - createdMonth)
⏳ past deadline when elapsed >= retentionMonths

Why: a retention deadline is a calendar concept, not a raw duration — computing it in months avoids drift.

items.prompt: Someone with raw database access edits event #4821 out of 9000 directly (bypassing the application's append() function). Per L3, what does verify() detect?
choices: Nothing — direct database edits are invisible to the hash chain
It flags #4821 as the first bad sequence, and every event from #4821 onward is also now provably inconsistent, since each depends on the hash of the one before it
It flags only the very last event in the log, #9000
It automatically repairs the tampered event back to its original value
items.explanation: Because each event's hash feeds into the next event's expected prevHash, tampering with #4821 breaks the link at #4821 and cascades forward — verify() reports the earliest broken point, giving investigators exactly where to start looking.
items.reference:
🔗 Each event's hash covers its own content + prevHash
🚨 Tampering anywhere breaks every link after it

Why: a hash chain turns a silent rewrite into a detectable one, pinpointing exactly where it happened.

items.prompt: Does the hash chain in L3 PREVENT someone with raw database access from editing a past event, or does it do something else?
choices: It fully prevents any edit from ever being made at the storage layer
It doesn't prevent the edit at the storage layer — it makes the edit detectable, by breaking the chain of hashes that verify() checks
It prevents edits only for events older than 30 days
It has no effect either way on raw database edits
items.explanation: Nothing running only inside the application can stop someone with direct database access from editing a row. What the chain provides is detection: verify() will notice the inconsistency and report where it started, turning a silent rewrite into a provable one.
items.reference:
🔗 Each event's hash covers its own content + prevHash
🚨 Tampering anywhere breaks every link after it

Why: a hash chain turns a silent rewrite into a detectable one, pinpointing exactly where it happened.

items.prompt: svc-analytics repeatedly requests a customer's SSN and is denied every time by the access gate, receiving only '[REDACTED].' Why does L3 say those denied attempts should still be logged?
choices: They shouldn't be — only successful reads matter for compliance
A pattern of repeated denied attempts is exactly the kind of signal a security investigation needs, and it's invisible if only successful reads are logged
Denied reads are logged only to satisfy storage quotas
Logging denied reads is required only for services owned by a different team
